question_text: In which stage of meiosis is the primary oocyte arrested?
explanation:
Explanation:

The primary oocyte is arrested in the diplotene stage of prophase I during fetal development and remains in this arrested phase until puberty. This arrest is regulated by oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), a substance secreted by granulosa cells, which prevents the oocyte from progressing further in meiosis until ovulation occurs.

Oogenesis and Meiotic Arrest:

question_text: Which of the following mechanisms plays a key role in preventing polyspermy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cortical reaction: After the sperm enters the egg, cortical granules in the egg release enzymes that modify the zona pellucida, preventing further sperm from binding and entering the egg, thus preventing polyspermy.

Explanation for other options:

Acrosome reaction (Option A): It helps the sperm penetrate the egg, not prevent polyspermy.

Zona reaction (Option C): Although it helps block other sperm after one has entered, the cortical reaction is the main process preventing polyspermy.

Capacitation (Option D): It enables sperm to fertilise the egg but does not directly prevent polyspermy.

question_text: An infertile couple walked into IVF clinic. FSH analogs were injected to induce follicular growth and hCG was injected to induce final oocyte maturation. The oocyte was then retrieved transvaginally. The oocyte thus retrieved is arrested at which of the following stages?
explanation:
The oocyte retrieved after final maturation is the secondary oocyte that is arrested in metaphase of meiosis Il.

If there is no fertilization, the secondary oocyte fails to complete the second meiotic division and degenerates about 24 hours after ovulation.

In in-vitro fertilization, initially, FSH analogs are administered to induce follicular growth. At this stage, the oocyte is arrested in the prophase stage of meiosis I. The final maturation of the oocyte is induced by the administration of hCG.

This causes the oocyte to resume the meiotic division, complete meiosis I, and enter meiosis II. However, the oocyte is arrested in the metaphase of meiosis Il until fertilization.

question_text: SRY gene is present in
explanation:
• The development of genital system begins during the fourth week of intrauterine life (IUL).
  • The genetic sex (genotype XY or XX) of embryo is established at time of fertilization, but gonads do not acquire male or female morphological characteristics till seventh week of the development.
  • Initially (week 1-6 of development) the gonads are structurally similar and hence this is called indifferent stage of gonad.
  • From seventh week onward, the development proceeds in different directions in males and females, and gonadal sex can then be determined morphologically.
  • By 12th week some male and female characteristics of the external genitalia can also be recognized.
  • By the end of 20th week phenotypical differentiation is complete.
  • This difference of development between male and female is because of chromosomal and hormonal factors.
  • The phenotypical differentiation is determined by SRY gene located on the short arm of Y chromosome (Yp11).
  • The SRY gene encodes for a protein called testis determining factor (TDF). The presence of TDF leads to development of male genital organs. As the indifferent gonad develops into the testis, the Leydig and Sertoli cells differentiate to produce testosterone and Mullerian inhibiting factor (MIF). This results in phenotypically male embryo.
  • In the absence of the TDF, testosterone, and MIF, the indifferent gonads will develop into ovary and embryo will be phenotypically female.

question_text: At the time of ovulation the secondary oocyte is in which of the following stage of meiotic division?
explanation:
Explanation:

At the time of ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase of the second meiotic division (metaphase II). It will complete meiosis II only after fertilization, upon penetration by a sperm.

Oogenesis

  • Primary Oocyte Formation:
    • Primary oocytes enter the first meiotic division before birth and complete it at puberty, just before ovulation.
    • No new primary oocytes are formed after birth.
  • Secondary Oocyte Stage:
    • The secondary oocyte is in the metaphase stage of the second meiotic division at the time of ovulation and continues until fertilization.
    • The secondary oocyte completes its meiotic division only upon fertilization.
  • Oocyte Count:
    • At birth, the ovary contains approximately two million germ cells.
    • By puberty, this number decreases to about 40,000 oocytes due to degeneration.
  • Ovulation During Reproductive Life:
    • Approximately 400-500 ovarian follicles undergo ovulation during a woman's reproductive life (ages 12-50).
    • About 5-30 primary oocytes mature and complete their first meiotic division before ovulation in each cycle.
  • Telophase (Option B): Occurs at the end of meiosis II, after fertilization, when the second polar body is formed.
  • Anaphase (Option C): Represents the separation of chromatids, which does not occur before fertilization in the oocyte.
  • Interphase (Option D): The oocyte does not enter interphase after meiosis I; it directly proceeds to meiosis II and is arrested at metaphase II until fertilization.

Key takeaways:

At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II of the second meiotic division and will only complete it if fertilized.

question_text: Identify the given structure
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image represents a blastocyst identified by outer trophoblast, inner cell mass and a cavity called blastocele.

The zygote undergoes a series of rapid mitotic divisions called cleavage to form the following structures:

  1. Morula: A solid ball of 16-32 cells. (Option A ruled out)
  2. Blastocyst: The morula develops a fluid-filled cavity (blastocoele) and differentiates into an inner cell mass (embryoblast) and an outer layer (trophoblast).
  3. Bilaminar Germ Disc: The embryoblast differentiates into two layers: epiblast and hypoblast.
  4. Trilaminar Germ Disc (Gastrula): The bilaminar disc undergoes gastrulation, forming three primary germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. (Option C ruled out)
  5. Neurula: The ectoderm forms the neural plate, which folds to create the neural groove and then the neural tube, marking the beginning of the central nervous system development. (Option D ruled out)

Key takeaway:

The blastocyst stage features a fluid-filled cavity called blastocele, outer trophoblast and inner cell mass, distinguishing it from the earlier morula and later gastrula and neurula stages.

question_text: Which of the following is embryonic period?
option_a: Beginning of 3rd week of intrauterine life to end of 8th week of intrauterine life.
option_b: End of 3rd week of intrauterine life to end of 8th week of intrauterine life.
option_c: Beginning of 3rd week of intrauterine life to Beginning of 8th week of intrauterine life.
option_d: End of 3rd week of intrauterine life to Beginning of 8th week of intrauterine life.
explanation:
Explanation:

The embryonic period extends from the beginning of the 3rd week to the end of the 8th week of intrauterine life. It represents the critical phase of organogenesis, during which all major organ systems begin to form from the three germ layers.

Stages of Development

  • Pre-Embryonic Period:
    • Duration: Conception to the end of the second week of intrauterine life (IUL).
    • Key Events:
      • Fertilization
      • Transport of zygote through the uterine tube
      • Mitotic divisions (cleavage)
      • Implantation
      • Formation of primordial embryonic tissues
  • Embryonic Period:
    • Duration: Beginning of the third week to the end of the eighth week of IUL.
    • Key Events:
      • Differentiation of germ layers into specific body organs
      • Formation of placenta, umbilical cord, and extraembryonic membranes
  • Fetal Period:
    • Duration: Beginning of the ninth week to birth.
    • Key Events: Tremendous growth and specialization of body structures

Key takeaways:

Prenatal development consists of the pre-embryonic period (conception to week 2), embryonic period (week 3 to week 8), and fetal period (week 9 to birth), with each stage involving key morphogenic events essential for growth and specialization.

question_text: The primitive streak first appears at the beginning of the ________ week.
explanation:

Epiblast cells form a thickening called the primitive streak, with a primitive knot or node located at its cranial end. Epiblast cells invaginate from this streak to form the mesoderm layer and to replace hypoblast with endoderm.

question_text: Absence of intraembryonic mesoderm at all the following sites, except;
explanation:
Explanation:

The primitive streak is the site where epiblast cells actively migrate inward during gastrulation to form intraembryonic mesoderm. Therefore, mesoderm is present in this region.

Formation of Intraembryonic Mesoderm:

  • Primitive Streak Formation: Cells of the primitive streak invaginate toward the endoderm, creating the primitive groove on its surface.
  • Intraembryonic Mesoderm Development: Cells from the primitive streak spread between the endoderm and ectoderm, forming the intraembryonic mesoderm, the third germ layer.
  • Direction of Spread: The intraembryonic mesoderm expands cranially, caudally, and laterally into all areas of the embryonic disc except in three specific regions.At the following sites, intraembryonic mesoderm is absent, and ectoderm and endoderm are directly fused:
    • Prochordal Plate: Ectoderm and endoderm are in close contact, forming the buccopharyngeal membrane.
    • Cloacal Membrane: Located at the caudal end of the disc, where ectoderm and endoderm are also in intimate contact, Future site of anus.
    • Notochord Region: Midline area between the prochordal plate and primitive knot, occupied by the notochord.

Key takeaways:

Intraembryonic mesoderm forms from invaginating cells of the primitive streak, spreading between endoderm and ectoderm, except in the prochordal plate, cloacal membrane, and notochord regions where the germ layers remain in contact.

question_text: The primitive streak completely disappears by the age of:
option_a: End of 2nd week of intrauterine life
option_b: End of 3rd week of intrauterine life
option_c: End of 4th week of intrauterine life
option_d: End of 5th week of intrauterine life
explanation:
Explanation:

The primitive streak appears around the 15th day of development and plays a key role in gastrulation, giving rise to intraembryonic mesoderm. It gradually regresses as the mesodermal migration completes and disappears by the end of the 4th week of intrauterine life.

The Primitive Streak:

  • Definition: A linear thickened band of ectodermal cells located at the caudal end of the embryo in the midline.
  • Formation: Results from the proliferation and migration of ectodermal cells on the embryonic disc's superior surface.
  • Characteristics: The cells of the primitive streak are pluripotent, capable of differentiating into various cell types.
  • Structures Derived:
    • Intraembryonic mesoderm
    • Septum transversum
    • Notochord
  • Determines the craniocaudal axis of the embryo
  • Demarcates the left and right halves of the embryo
  • Fate of the Primitive Streak:
    • Actively forms intraembryonic mesoderm through cell ingression until the end of the third week of intrauterine life (IUL).
    • Regresses craniocaudally and disappears by the end of the fourth week or becomes insignificant in the sacrococcygeal region.

Key takeaways:

The primitive streak is a midline band of ectodermal cells that forms key structures like intraembryonic mesoderm and notochord, determines the embryo's axes, and regresses by the end of the fourth week.

  • Onset: The first somite pair appears in the occipital region on Day 20, shortly after which subsequent pairs form in a craniocaudal
  • Formation Sequence:
    • Cranial somite are the oldest; caudal somite is the approximately 38 pairs of somite form between Days 20 and 30 of development (the somite period).

explanation:
Neural crest cells give rise to the peripheral parts of the autonomic nervous system, which includes all sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia. Neural crest cells form all sensory ganglia of the peripheral nervous system. Neural crest cells also populate the adrenal medulla.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Central Nervous System Embryology Page number - 287

question_text: Identify the marked structure in the developing embryo.
explanation:
Explanation:

The primitive streak is the first structure to appear during gastrulation, visible as a linear midline thickening in the epiblast. It serves as the site for epiblast cell migration, which leads to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The primitive streak establishes the cranial-caudal axis and is essential for proper embryonic patterning.

Primitive Streak and Its Role in Gastrulation:


Explanation of other options:

Notochord (Option B): Incorrect . The notochord forms later from mesodermal cells after the establishment of the primitive streak and acts as a signaling center for neural tube development.

Neural groove (Option C): Incorrec. The neural groove forms during neurulation, when the neural plate invaginates to create the neural tube, which occurs after gastrulation.

Secondary neural plate (Option D): Incorrect. The secondary neural plate contributes to secondary neurulation, forming the caudal neural tube, and is not involved in early gastrulation.

question_text: Which of the following adult structures is derived from the notochord?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The notochord is a midline mesodermal structure that appears during early embryogenesis.
  • It plays a critical role as a signalling centre, inducing the overlying ectoderm to form the neural tube.
  • Although most of the notochord degenerates, its remnants persist in the adult intervertebral disc as the nucleus pulposus.

Explanation of other options:

Annulus fibrosus (Option B): This develops from mesenchymal cells of the sclerotome, not from the notochord.

Neural tube (Option C): Induced by the notochord but derived from ectoderm, not the notochord itself.

Septum transversum (Option D): Gives rise to part of the diaphragm and connective tissue of the liver, and is not related to the notochord.

question_text: What is the significance of primitive streak?
option_a: It allows for the differentiation between the three layers of trilaminar disc
option_b: It allows for differentiation between caudal and cranial ends of epiblast
option_c: It specifically extends cranially and caudally to form oropharyngeal membrane and cloacal membrane
option_d: It forms the 4 limbs of the body
explanation:
The primitive streak is a linear band of thickened epiblast that first appears at the caudal end of embryo and grows cranially. It proliferates to form the primitive knot or node. It is then possible to distinguish cranial (knot) and caudal (streak) ends of embryo. It does not specifically extend to form oropharyngeal membrane and cloacal membrane. Mesenchymal cells migrate from primitive knot to form notochordal process which then extend to form oropharyngeal membrane and cloacal membrane.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 51

question_text: Mesoderm lateral to the notochord:
explanation:
The mesoderm lateral to the notochord arises from invagination of the epiblast at the primitive streak during the third week. Some of this mesoderm forms angiogenic clusters and migrates cranially to reach the cardiogenic area in front of the prochordal plate. Ganglia are from neural crest, which is ectodermal.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 51

question_text: Developmental defects in the neural crest cells will give rise to defective development of all the following structures, except;
explanation:
Explanation:

The adrenal cortex comes from the mesoderm, making it the correct exception in this case.

  • Neural crest cells originate from the neurectoderm and give rise to several structures, including:
    • Dorsal root ganglia
    • Sensory ganglia of cranial nerves
    • Autonomic ganglia
    • Adrenal medulla and chromaffin tissue
    • Melanocytes and Schwann cells
  • Dorsal root ganglia and autonomic gangliaare derived from neural crest cells, which are crucial for sensory and autonomic nervous system development (Option A& B).
  • Chromaffin tissue,which is part of the adrenal medulla, is also derived from neural crest cells (Option D).

Key takeaway:

Defects in neural crest cells affect structures like dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, and chromaffin tissue, but not the adrenal cortex, which is mesodermal in origin.

question_text: All are derived from ectoderm except -
explanation: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Adrenal cortex [Ref Inderbir Singh Human Embryology Sth/e p. 300] The cells of the adrenal cortex arise from the coelomic epithelium (mesoderm).  The cells of the medulla are derived from the neural crest cells (ectoderm). The anterior pituitary is derived from the surface ectoderm lining the oral cavity as it is an outgrowth from the Rathke's pouch. The posterior pituitary is actually a continuation of the hypothalamus and so it is derived from the neural ectoderm.· The spinal cord and brain are derived from the neural ectoderm. The retina is also derived from the neural ectoderm.

question_text: Which of the following structure of the eye develops from surface ectoderm?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lens develops from the surface ectoderm of the head. The surface ectoderm also forms the anterior epithelium of the cornea.

Adult components of eye derived from various embryonic structures:

Key points:

  • The eye develops from four sources:
  • Neuroectoderm of forebrain
  • Surface ectoderm of head
  • Mesoderm between neuroectoderm of forebrain and surface ectoderm of head
  • Neural crest cells

Key Takeaway:

The lens is derived from surface ectoderm, while other structures such as the sclera, iris epithelium, and vitreous body come from neuroectoderm, mesoderm, and neural crest cells respectively.

question_text: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
explanation:
Explanation:

The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is not derived from neural crest cells. It originates from the outer layer of the optic cup, which develops from the neural ectoderm (a derivative of the neural tube). The RPE functions to absorb scattered light and maintain photoreceptor health but does not share the neural crest origin of other ocular tissues.

Derivatives of Neural Crest Cells:


Explanation of other options:

Ciliary muscles (Option A): Derived from neural crest cells; these smooth muscles control the shape of the lens for accommodation.

Ciliary ganglion (Option C): Derived from neural crest cells; this parasympathetic ganglion is associated with the oculomotor nerve and innervates the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscles.

Melanocytes (Option D): Derived from neural crest cells; these pigment-producing cells are distributed in the skin, uveal tract, and other regions of the body.

question_text: Of the following, which is derived from endoderm?
explanation:
The epithelium of the pharynx is epithelium that is derived from the endodermal epithelium of the primitive gut. The epithelium of the lower part of the anal canal is derived from ectoderm, while the upper part is lined with endoderm. The boundary between endodermal and ectodermal lining is called the pectinate line.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 51

question_text: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak?
explanation:
Explanation:

During gastrulation, the epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to establish the three germ layers, endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.
The first group of migrating epiblast cells displaces the hypoblast and forms the definitive endoderm. This is followed by additional epiblast cells that migrate between the epiblast and endoderm to form the intraembryonic mesoderm. The cells that remain in the epiblast layer ultimately form the ectoderm.

Gastrulation and Germ Layer Formation:

Explanation of other options:

Cardiac mesoderm (Option B): Incorrect. It develops from the mesoderm, which forms after the endoderm.

Epidermis (Option C): Incorrect. It is derived from the ectoderm, the last germ layer to form.

Neural groove (Option D): Incorrect. It arises later from the ectoderm during neurulation, after gastrulation is complete.

question_text: Which of the following is not a derivative of ectoderm?
option_a: Epithelial lining of external auditory meatus
option_b: Epithelial lining of middle ear cavity
explanation:
Explanation:

Epithelial lining of the middle ear cavity is not derived from ectoderm; it is derived from the endoderm.

Derivatives of three germ layers are as follow:

Key takeaways:

The epithelial lining of the middle ear cavity is derived from the endoderm, while the other options (external auditory meatus, nasal cavity, and oral cavity) are derived from the ectoderm.

question_text: Which of the following structures is derived from paraxial mesoderm of the cervical region?
option_c: Skeletal muscle of the upper limb
explanation:
Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites, which give rise to the axial skeleton and connective tissues of the trunk, all skeletal muscle, and the dermis. In the lower cervical regions, the somitic myotomes form the skeletal muscle of the developing upper limb. The eleventh thoracic vertebra is sclerotomal (somitic), but from lower thoracic levels.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 51

question_text: Which of the following is correct about the arrangement of structures before folding of the embryo?
option_a: Septum transversum lies caudal to the pericardial cavity and heart tube
option_b: Cranial part of the neural plate lies above and behind the primitive buccopharyngeal membrane
option_c: Heart tube lies below the pericardial cavity
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cranial part of the neural plate lies above and behind the primitive buccopharyngeal membrane
  • Before folding, the embryo is a flat trilaminar disc.
  • The cranial part of the neural plate (which will give rise to the brain) lies cranial (above) and dorsal (behind) the buccopharyngeal membrane (future mouth region).
  • This is the normal topographic arrangement in the pre-folded stage - the neural plate is dorsal, and the buccopharyngeal membrane is ventral and slightly anterior.

Arrangement of important structures of embryo before and after the folding in craniocaudal direction as follows:


  • Before folding, the septum transversum is actually located cranial to the pericardial cavity and heart tube, not caudal. During cephalocaudal folding, it shifts to a position between the thoracic cavity and abdominal cavity, becoming the future diaphragm (Option A).
  • The heart tube lies ventral to (in front of) the pericardial cavity before folding, not below it. The pericardial cavity is a space dorsal to the heart tube in the early embryo (Option C).
  • The allantois develops as a diverticulum from the posterior wall of the yolk sac, and before folding, it extends dorsally and caudally toward the connecting stalk (future umbilical cord). It is not ventrally directed (Option D).

Key takeaways:

The septum transversum is above the pericardial cavity, the cranial neural plate is behind the buccopharyngeal membrane, the heart tube is anterior to the pericardial cavity, and the allantois is a ventral outpouching forming part of the urinary bladder and umbilical cord.

question_text: Mesodermal in origin ?
explanation: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Microglial cells [Ref I.B. singh p. 319-321] Microglial cells are the nervous system counterpart of the monocyte macrophage system. The unique feature about microglia is that unlike other neuroglial cells it is not developed from neuroectoderm. These cells are mesodermal in origin.

question_text: During the period of development of the major organ systems, development and differentiation appear first in what region?
explanation:
In the development of the cardiovascular, nervous, digestive and musculoskeletal systems, differentiation generally occurs in a cranial to caudal progression.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 51

question_text: Which layer invades into the maternal endometrium and forms the lacunar network for placental-maternal exchange?
explanation:
The syncytiotrophoblast layer formed from the trophoblast invades the maternal endometrium. It comes into contact with blood vessels and forms lacunae, spaces filled with maternal blood. This forms the lacunar network that functions in the exchange of nutrients and waste products between mother and fetus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 43

question_text: Which layer is acellular, does not expand mitotically, and produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) which stimulates progesterone production by the corpus luteum?
explanation:
Syncytiotrophoblast is acellular, does not expand mitotically, and produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) which stimulates progesterone production by the corpus luteum. B-hCG produced can be detected in maternal blood as early as day 10 of pregnancy and is part of the pregnancy test. Cytotrophoblast is cellular, expands mitotically into syncytiotrophoblast to form primary chorionic villi that can be used in chorionic villus sampling that is genetic testing for the early fetus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 43

question_text: Which layer is cellular and expands mitotically into syncytiotrophoblast to form primary chorionic villi that can be used in chorionic villus sampling or genetic testing for the early fetus?
explanation:
Cytotrophoblast is cellular, expands mitotically into syncytiotrophoblast to form primary chorionic villi that can be used in chorionic villus sampling that is genetic testing for the early fetus. Syncytiotrophoblast is acellular, does not expand mitotically, and produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) which stimulates progesterone production by the corpus luteum. B-hCG produced can be detected in maternal blood as early as day 10 of pregnancy and is part of the pregnancy test.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 43

question_text: The definitive yolk sac of the embryo appears by what day?
explanation:
Around the 13th day, the definitive yolk sac is formed by the hypoblast cells that line the inside of the exocoelomic membrane.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 43

question_text: The allantois is derived from:
explanation:
The allantois is an endodermal outpouching of the yolk sac. Early on, it is attached to the hindgut, but when the urorectal septum divides the cloaca, it becomes associated with the urinary bladder and contributes to its development. The allantois forms the urachus and then the median umbilical ligament.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: The yolk sac detaches from the gut by the end of the:
explanation:
Through body folding, the yolk sac separates from the gut during the 5th week, although the gut remains attached to the yolk sac by the vitelline duct, which persists into the third month of development.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Implantation of the embryo in the lower uterus can cause what medical condition that may lead to hemorrhage, fetal insufficiency, and even death for both mother and baby due to obstruction of the birth canal?
explanation:
Implantation of the embryo in the lower uterus can cause placenta previa, in which the placenta obstructs the birth canal. If Cesarean section is not performed, it can lead to hemorrhage, fetal insufficiency, and even death.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 29

question_text: Which of the following is false about monozygotic twins?
explanation:
Explanation:

Monoamniotic & dichorionic combination is impossible, because if there are two chorions (dichorionic), there must be two amnions, and the amnion always forms inside the chorion.

Differences between monozygotic and dizygotic twins

  • Diamniotic & monochorionic (Option A):This occurs when the zygote splits between days 4–8 (after chorion formation but before amnion formation).Hence, twins share one chorion (monochorionic) but have two amniotic sacs (diamniotic).This is the most common type of monozygotic twinning (~70%).
  • Diamniotic & dichorionic (Option B): Occurs when the zygote splits within the first 3 days after fertilization, before the formation of the chorion. Each twin forms its own chorion and amnion forming dichorionic, diamniotic. These can resemble dizygotic twins but are still identical genetically.
  • Monoamniotic & monochorionic (Option D): Occurs when splitting happens between days 8-13, after both amnion and chorion have formed. Both twins share the same amniotic sac and chorion. This type carries a high risk of cord entanglement.

Key takeaways:

Monozygotic twins can exhibit various configurations depending on the timing of zygotic splitting, resulting in diamniotic and dichorionic, or monoamniotic and monochorionic conditions. Understanding these differences is crucial in prenatal care and monitoring for potential complications.

question_text: What is the type of human placenta?
explanation:
Explanation:

In human's maternal blood is separated from fetal blood by chorionic tissue; hence human placenta is termed hemochorial.

Phylogenic classification of placenta:

  • It is based on maternal and fetal tissues that come in contact.
  • Phylogenetically the placenta is classified into following five types.

Key takeaways:

The human placenta is classified as hemochorial, where maternal blood is in direct contact with chorionic tissue. This classification is part of a broader phylogenetic system that categorizes placentas based on the interaction of maternal and fetal tissues.

question_text: Which of the following is not a content of umbilical cord?
explanation:
Explanation:

The umbilical cord normally contains four main structures:

  • 2 umbilical arteries which carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta.
  • 1 umbilical vein which carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.
  • Wharton’s jelly (a mucoid connective tissue) surrounding them.
  • Allantoic duct remnant (sometimes visible microscopically).

The Umbilical Cord:

  • Structure: A cord-like structure connecting the fetus to the uterine wall via the placenta.
  • Extends from the umbilicus of the fetus to the center of the fetal surface of the placenta.
  • Covered by a glistening amniotic membrane.
  • Twisting and Features: The cord is twisted and may present false knots.
  • Contents:
    • Two umbilical arteries: Carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta.
    • One umbilical vein: Typically, the left umbilical vein, carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.
    • Wharton's jelly: A gelatinous substance that provides cushioning.
    • Remains of allantoic diverticulum: A remnant of the allantois, involved in early excretion and respiration.
    • Remains of Vitello intestinal duct: A remnant of the yolk sac.
  • Development: The right umbilical vein typically disappears by the end of the first trimester.

Key takeaways:

The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta, containing two umbilical arteries, one left umbilical vein, Wharton's jelly, and remnants of the allantoic diverticulum and Vitello intestinal duct, all encased in the amniotic membrane.

question_text: Median umbilical ligament is a remnant of:
explanation:
Explanation:

Median umbilical ligament is a remnant of the allantois. During fetal development, the allantois connects the developing bladder to the umbilicus. After birth, the allantois obliterates and forms a fibrous cord called the urachus, which later becomes the median umbilical ligament.

Remnants of Fetal Structures:

  • Vitellointestinal duct (Option A):Remnant is Meckel's diverticulum.
  • Allantois : Becomes the median umbilical ligament.
  • Umbilical artery (Option C):Forms the superior vesicle artery and medial umbilical ligament.
  • Left umbilical vein (Option D): Becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis.

Remnants of fetal structures after birth:

Key Takeaway:

The median umbilical ligament is a fibrous remnant of the allantois, part of the urinary development system.

question_text: Each of the following ligaments in the adult are derived from fetal blood vessels EXCEPT:
option_c: Round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis)
explanation:
Median umbilical ligament, attaching to upper part of bladder, is a remnant of the urachus, which itself was a remnant of the allantois. The allantois was a connection between the urinary bladder and the yolk sac, not a fetal blood vessel.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 195

question_text: Upon the delivery of a term newborn, a thorough examination of the umbilical cord reveals crucial information. What are the essential components of a healthy umbilical cord?
explanation:
Explanation:

A typical umbilical cord of a newborn full-term baby contains two arteries and one vein.

  • 3 veins each draining into the right and left horns of the sinus venosus:
    • Common cardinal vein
    • Umbilical vein
    • Vitelline vein
  • Umbilical veins are coming from the placenta. Later in the fetal circulation, the right umbilical vein regresses, and only the left umbilical vein is left. (Option B, C, and D ruled out)
  • The persisting left umbilical vein in the fetal circulation also degenerates and forms the ligamentum teres of the liver (having no function at all).
  • Vitelline veins drain the yolk sac, which forms the gut tube.
  • The right and left vitelline veins pass through the septum transversum.
  • The septum transversum breaks the vitelline veins into right and left hepatic-cardiac channels.
  • The right hepatic-cardiac channel later contributes to form the terminal part of the IVC, which carries the blood from the liver towards the heart.
  • The right vitelline vein (along with some contribution from the left vitelline vein) forms the portal vein.

question_text: Each pharyngeal arch includes:
option_a: Derivatives of ectodermal neural crest cells
option_c: A mesodermal core from paraxial mesoderm
explanation:
The pharyngeal arches have their own mesodermal core, giving rise to cartilaginous & muscular components, cranial nerve components, vascular components and derivatives of neural crest cells, which supplement much of the connective tissue of the face.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Stylopharyngeus is derived from which pharyngeal arch?
explanation:
Explanation:

The stylopharyngeus muscle is the only muscle derived from the third pharyngeal arch.

It is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), which is the nerve of the 3rd arch.

Key takeaways:

Stylopharyngeus muscle is derived from the third pharyngeal arch and is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Each pharyngeal arch gives rise to specific muscle groups, with the first arch associated with mastication, the second with facial expression, and the fourth with pharyngeal constriction.

question_text: Second pharyngeal pouch gives development to:
explanation:
Explanation:

The second pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the epithelial lining of the palatine tonsil and forms the tonsillar fossa (or intratonsillar cleft).

Derivatives of the 2nd Pharyngeal Pouch:

  • The endoderm of the 2nd pouch proliferates to form buds that are invaded by lymphoid tissue from the mesoderm.
  • This ultimately develops into the palatine tonsil.
  • The remnant of the pouch persists as the tonsillar (intratonsillar) cleft.

Derivatives of pharyngeal pouches:


  • Ultimo-pharyngeal body (Option A): Derived from the 5th pharyngeal pouch (often considered part of the 4th). Gives rise to the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland.
  • Superior parathyroid gland (Option C): Derived from the 4th pharyngeal pouch.
  • Inferior parathyroid gland (Option D): Derived from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch (along with the thymus).

question_text: The result of failure of fusion of the first and second branchial arches leads to development of:
explanation:
Explanation:

Preauricular sulcus:

The result of failure of fusion of the first and second branchial arches.

Clinically, pre-auricular sinuses may become chronically infected and require surgical excision.

This may be technically demanding, given the close proximity to the facial nerve and auricular tubercles around the dorsal end of the first branchial cleft.


Branchial cyst (Option A): Forms from remnants of the second, third, and fourth pharyngeal clefts, not from failure of fusion of the first and second arches.

Diminutive ear (Option C): Microtia is an isolated congenital anomaly related to external ear development, not directly associated with branchial arch fusion failure.

Satiro's ear (Option D): A deformity of the auricle due to cartilage abnormalities leading to elf like abnormalities, not due to branchial arch fusion

Key Takeaway:

The pre-auricular sinus is the result of the failure of fusion of the first and second branchial arches, leading to the formation of small pits near the ear, which may become infected and need surgical excision.

question_text: Which of the following arises from 6th pharyngeal arch?
explanation:
Explanation :

  • The ductus arteriosus arises from the sixth pharyngeal arch
  • The ductus arteriosus is a fetal blood vessel that connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta, allowing a portion of oxygenated blood to bypass the developing fetal lungs.
  • This shunt helps direct oxygenated blood towards the systemic circulation while the lungs are not yet fully functional in the prenatal period.

Derivatives of Pharyngeal arches

question_text: The anomaly demonstrated in the image is due to a developmental defect in which of the following pharyngeal arch arteries?
explanation:
Explanation:

The condition shown in the image is Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA), a congenital heart defect where the ductus arteriosus (a fetal blood vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta) fails to close after birth.

  • The ductus arteriosus is derived from the left 6th pharyngeal arch artery.

explanation: Ans. is `c' i.e., Stapes om

question_text: Calcium homeostasis disturbance is seen in
explanation: Answer- A. Malignant hyperthermia Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic condition caused due to mutation of the "Ryanodine receptor gene". Ryanodine receptor gene controls the level of "cytosolic calcium" and therefore skeletal muscle contraction.

question_text: A small blind pit at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle that drips mucus is likely the persistence of the embryonic opening of the:
option_d: Second branchial groove and cervical sinus
explanation:
The question describes a lateral cervical cyst that is draining by way of a branchial fistula. This forms due to a failure of the 2nd arch to grow caudally over the third and fourth arches, and causes the persistence of the opening of the 2nd branchial groove and the cervical sinus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Which of the following are associated with the 3rd pharyngeal pouch?
option_a: Parafollicular or calcitonin cells of the thyroid gland
explanation:
The 3rd pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus gland. The parafollicular cells are from the ultimobranchial body of the 5th pharyngeal pouch. Thyroid arises from the epithelium of the pharynx, via the thyroid diverticulum

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Auditory ossicles develop from the condensed mesenchyme of the:
explanation:
The auditory ossicles form from the mesenchyme of the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches. Malleus & incus come from the 1st arch, while stapes arises from the 2nd arch.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Identify the correct associations:
option_a: External ear abnormality - mandibular and maxillary processes
option_b: Oblique facial cleft - frontal and maxillary processes
option_c: Cleft lip - maxillary & medial nasal processes
explanation:
Macro- and microstomia results from too little or too much fusion between maxillary and mandibular swellings. Oblique facial cleft represents failure of maxillary & lateral nasal process fusion. External ear develops from first pharyngeal cleft region dorsally. Cleft lip is usually between maxillary & medial nasal prominences.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 278

question_text: Which of the following malformations is NOT found in the "first pharyngeal arch syndrome"?
explanation:
Connective tissue of the first arch gives rise to incus and malleus of the middle ear, the premaxilla, maxilla, zygomatic, part of the temporal bone and Meckel's cartilage for mandible development. First arch syndrome can involve various components of the face and ear.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: The given image shown defect in development of which pharyngeal arch?
explanation:
(complete absence of the ear pinna) occurs due to the defect in the development of 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches. The pinna develops from 6 tissue elevations called the auricular hillocks formed around the margins of the dorsal portion of the 1st pharyngeal cleft.

  • 3 hillocks are from the 1st pharyngeal (mandibular) arch
  • 3 hillocks are from the 2nd pharyngeal (hyoid) arch.

The mandibular arch contributes to the tragus of the pinna only, while the rest of the pinna is derived from the hyoid arch. Invagination of the first pharyngeal arch gives rise to the external auditory meatus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: The tubotympanic recess gives rise to which structure?
explanation:
The tubotympanic recess forms the auditory tube.

Development of the Middle Ear:

  • The distal part of the 1st pharyngeal pouch becomes the tubotympanic recess.
  • The tubotympanic recess gives rise to the primitive tympanic cavity distally, while the proximal part remains narrow and forms the auditory tube (eustachian tube). It also forms the lining of the middle ear cavity.
  • The 3 ossicles are formed from mesenchymal condensations from the 1st pharyngeal arch (malleus and incus) and 2nd pharyngeal arch (stapes).
  • The tympanic membrane is formed where the ectoderm of the 1st pharyngeal cleft dips to meet the endoderm of the 1st pharyngeal pouch, with contribution from the intervening mesoderm.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Ear Embryology Page number - 321

question_text: A newborn is diagnosed with Treacher Collin's syndrome. Abnormality in the development of which of the following pharyngeal arches will most likely lead to the given condition?
explanation:
First arch syndromes are congenital defects caused due to the failure of the neural crest cells to migrate into the 1st pharyngeal arch.

They are:

  • Treacher-Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) - Autosomal dominant genetic disorder characterized by:
  • Craniofacial bone defects - Involves mandible (causing micrognathia), maxilla, and zygomatic arches
  • Ear defects - Involves the external ear, atresia of auditory canals, and abnormalities of the middle ear ossicles leading to bilateral conductive hearing loss
  • Eye defects - Down-slanting palpebral fissures and lower eyelid colobomas.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e.,Stapedial artery [Ref Garg 2"/e - 223; Langman's - 185] 2nd (hyoid Stapedial artery arch) : 3rd:- Common carotid/internal carotid 4th:- : Right 4th aortic arch, subclavian artery, Left 4th aortic  arch: aortic arch 6th:- Right aortic arch: pulmonary artery, Left 6th aortic  arch: Pulmonary artstxand ductus arteriosus

question_text: A newborn had hypoplasia of the mandibles and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, and slanted palpebral fissures. Abnormality in the development of which of the following pharyngeal arches will most likely lead to the given condition?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

The clinical presentation is characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome. This condition results from a defective development of the first pharyngeal arch, which gives rise to the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bones, and associated structures of the lower face and jaw.

First arch syndromes are a group of congenital conditions resulting from the failed migration or development of neural crest cells into the first pharyngeal arch.

A prime example is Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder with an incidence of approximately 1 in 50,000 live births. The syndrome is characterized by a constellation of craniofacial defects stemming from abnormal first pharyngeal arch development.

Key features include:

  • Craniofacial Bone Defects: Underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the zygomatic bones, mandible, and maxilla.
  • Ear Abnormalities: These range from a narrow or completely absent external auditory canal (aural atresia) to malformations of the middle ear ossicles (malleus and incus). These structural defects are a direct cause of bilateral conductive hearing loss.
  • Eye Defects: Characteristic downward-slanting palpebral fissures and notches (colobomas) in the lower eyelids.

Explanation of other options:

Pharyngeal arch 2 (Option B): This arch primarily forms structures derived from Reichert's cartilage (e.g., stapes, styloid process, parts of the hyoid bone) and is not responsible for mandibular or zygomatic development.

Pharyngeal arch 3 (Option C): This arch contributes to the formation of the greater horn of the hyoid bone and the stylopharyngeus muscle, not the facial bones.

Pharyngeal arch 4 (Option D): This arch gives rise to laryngeal cartilages and certain pharyngeal muscles and is not involved in the development of the described facial structures.

question_text: Which of the following develops from the connective tissue component of the second pharyngeal arch?
explanation:
The connective tissue of the second pharyngeal arch develops into stapedius, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn of the hyoid, and the upper portion of the body of the hyoid bone.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: An absent lower jaw is called:
explanation:
The total absence of a lower jaw is termed agnathus. There is a class of fishes called agnatha with no lower jaw development.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 278

question_text: Which structure develop from the 6th pharyngeal arch artery on the left side?
explanation:
Explanation :

  • The 6th pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to:
    • Left side: Ductus arteriosus and proximal left pulmonary artery
    • Right side: Right pulmonary artery
  • The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta during fetal life, allowing blood to bypass the lungs.
  • After birth, it normally closes to form the ligamentum arteriosum.

Explanation of Other Options:

Arch of Aorta (Option A): Derived from the 4th pharyngeal arch artery (left side), not the 6th.

Carotid arteries (Option C): Derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch artery, including common carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries.

Subclavian artery (Option D): Derived from the right 4th pharyngeal arch artery, along with part of the dorsal aorta and 7th intersegmental artery.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Pharyngeal Arch Artery Derivatives
  • Clinical Correlation:
    • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): Persistence of the left 6th arch derivative after birth, leading to left-to-right shunt.
    • Understanding arch artery derivatives is essential in congenital heart defect surgery and interpreting neonatal echocardiograms.

question_text: A 1-year-old baby with loss of pharyngeal reflex was diagnosed to have infantile progressive bulbar palsy. Which of the following gives rise to the affected structure?
explanation:
In infantile progressive bulbar palsy, the affected structure is the medulla oblongata. It arises from the rhombocephalon (hindbrain).

The rhombencephalon is further subdivided into a cranial part (metencephalon) and a caudal part (myelencephalon)

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Central Nervous System Embryology Page number - 297

question_text: The third branchial arch cartilage gives rise to the:
option_d: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
explanation:
The third arch produces the lower part of the body and the greater horns of the hyoid bone, as well as the stylopharyngeus muscle. Its nerve is the glossopharyngeal nerve. The sphenomandibular ligament is from the 1st arch. The styloid process & stylohyoid ligament are from the 2nd arch. Thyroid cartilage is from 4th arch.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: A patient presents with a cyst on the neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid at the junction of the upper and middle third of the muscle. This cyst is due to the persistence of which of the following embryological clefts?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The second pharyngeal cleft, located between the second and third arches, normally contributes to the formation of a temporary structure called the cervical sinus.
  • This sinus usually disappears, but if it persists, it can result in the development of a branchial cyst in the described location.

Explanation of Other Options:

1st cleft (Option A): Forms the external auditory canal when it persists; not responsible for lateral neck cysts.

3rd cleft (Option C): Lies between the third and fourth arches, but persistence does not cause cysts at the sternocleidomastoid level.

4th cleft (Option D): Involved in the lower pharyngeal region; persistence does not produce cysts at the described site.

question_text: Branchial cysts or lateral cervical cysts:
option_a: Are found along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
option_b: Are formed from a rupture of the membrane between pharyngeal pouches and branchial clefts
option_c: Are remnants of the thyroglossal duct
option_d: Are found in front of the ear
explanation:
Lateral cervical cysts are remnants of the cervical sinus, which forms when the 2nd arch grows over the 3rd & 4th arches. The cysts are found along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, usually just below the angle of the jaw. They have nothing to do with the rupture of anything.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: The fact that general and special sensory information from the posterior part of the tongue is carried by glossopharyngeal nerve indicates that this part of tongue is from branchial arch ____.
explanation:
Hypobranchial eminence forms the posterior third of the tongue. It is served by the nerve of the 3rd branchial arch, glossopharyngeal, or cranial nerve IX. Glossopharyngeal carries general sense and the special sense of taste from this part of the tongue. In anterior tongue, trigeminal does general and facial does special sense.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 273

question_text: The embryonic branchial arch arteries give origin to all of the following postnatal structures EXCEPT:
explanation:
Aortic arch is derived from aortic sac and left fourth arch. The ligamentum arteriosum is from the distal portion of the left sixth arch, from which the pulmonary arteries also arise. Common carotids come from third arch. The ascending aorta, however, is from the truncus arteriosus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Which of the following structures is NOT part of the 2nd branchial arch?
option_b: Superior portion of body of hyoid bone
explanation:
The cartilage of the first arch gives rise to malleus, incus, spine of sphenoid & lingula of mandible. Sphenomandibular ligament is a remnant of the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage, also from the first arch. Second arch cartilage gives rise to stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser horns & upper part of hyoid.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Which of the following structures is NOT part of the first branchial arch?
explanation:
Mandibular and maxillary processes are both from first arch, as are malleus & incus bones of the ear. Sphenomandibular ligament is the remnant of the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage, around which the mandible forms. Second arch cartilage gives rise to stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser horns & upper part of hyoid.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: The mesenchymal cells which aggregate to form blood islands are called:
explanation:
Angioblasts are the cells that form the blood islands. These blood islands then develop into the blood cells and the endothelium of the blood vessels. This early blood cell and blood vessel formation occurs first in the extraembryonic mesoderm of the yolk sac, chorion and connecting stalk.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: By 13-14 days of development, angiogenic cell clusters have differentiated in the:
option_b: Splanchnic mesoderm in the wall of the yolk sac
explanation:
Angiogenic cell clusters develop in all of these areas, giving rise to the cardiovascular system in the embryo. Within the embryo, the angiogenic cell clusters are found in the horse-shoe shaped region beneath the intraembryonic coelom. Cranial to the prochordal plate lies the cardiogenic region, part of this larger area.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 162

question_text: The sinus venosus:
option_a: Has a right horn which persists in the adult as the coronary sinus
option_b: Has a left venous valve which develops into the valve of the coronary sinus
option_c: Forms the smooth-walled portion of the adult right atrium
option_d: Receives blood from common cardinal veins, Umbilical veins and Vitelline veins.
explanation:
3 veins each draining into the right and left horn of the sinus venosus:

  • Common cardinal vein
  • Umbilical vein
  • Vitelline vein

Umbilical veins are coming from the placenta. Later in the fetal circulation, the right umbilical vein regresses and only the left umbilical vein is left.

The persisting left umbilical vein in the fetal circulation also degenerates and forms ligamentum teres of the liver (having no function at all).

Vitelline veins drain the yolk sac, which forms the gut tube.

The right and left vitelline veins are passing through the septum transversum.

The septum transversum breaks the vitelline veins into right and left hepatic-cardiac channels.

Right hepatic-cardiac channel later contributes to form the terminal part of the IVC, which carries the blood from the liver towards the heart.

Right vitelline vein (along with some contribution from the left vitelline vein) forms the portal vein.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: In normal fetal circulation:
option_a: The umbilical arteries carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo
option_b: The foramen ovale shunts oxygenated blood from the left to the right side of the heart
option_c: Blood can enter the pulmonary circulation via the ductus arteriosus
option_d: Blood from the placenta bypasses the sinusoidal plexus of the liver in the ductus venosus
explanation:
Oxygenated blood from the placenta is carried via the umbilical veins. This blood bypasses the liver sinusoids via the ductus venosus. Upon reaching the heart, oxygenated blood can be shunted from right to left via the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus also passes blood from pulmonary to systemic circuits.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The specialized group of mesenchymal cells which aggregate to form blood islands are called:
explanation:
The mesenchymal stem cells that aggregate to form blood islands are Angioblasts. These angioblasts arise from Hemangioblasts during a process called 'Vasculogenesis'

Hemoblasts is a tempting choice, but the blood cell and blood vessel precursors are called angioblasts. Angioblasts form angiogenic cell clusters, which form blood islands centrally and primitive blood vessels peripherally. Early angiogenesis occurs in chorion, yolk sac & connecting stalk, but involves only mesodermal cells.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 162

question_text: Fossa ovalis closes because of fusion of ?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Septum primum + Septum secundum [Ref Essentials of human embryology — 213-215] After birth, the foramen ovale closes by fusion of septum primum with septum secundum.

question_text: The embryonic origin of the ligamentum arteriosum is from the:
explanation:
The sixth arch is the pulmonary arch, from which pulmonary arteries are derived. On the left side, this arch maintains its connection with the dorsal aorta. In the fetus, this connection is patent and is called the ductus arteriosus. Postnatally, it closes and persists as the ligamentum arteriosum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 162

question_text: A newborn developed cyanosis soon after birth. Chest X-ray showed the characteristic egg-on-a-string appearance. Which of the following mechanisms during embryonic development will most likely lead to the given condition?
option_a: Non-fusion of aortico-pulmonary septum with truncus arteriosus
option_c: Failure of cono-truncal ridge to fuse and descend
option_d: Aortico-pulmonary septum not following its spiral course
explanation:
The egg-on-a-string appearance on chest X-ray is characteristically seen in the transposition of great arteries (TGA). It is considered to arise due to abnormal spiraling of the aortopulmonary septum (conotruncal septum).

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 171

question_text: The limbus fossa ovalis is the remnant of
explanation:
The limbus fossa ovalis (also known as annulus ovalis represents the remnant of the lower free edge of the septum secundum.

Fossa ovalis is an oval-shaped depression in the septal wall of the right atrium just above the opening of inferior vena cava. It marks the location of embryonic foramen ovale.

  • The floor of fossa ovalis is the remnant of septum primum.
  • The limbus of fossa ovalis is the prominent upper margin of the fossa ovalis and a remnant of the septum secundum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: In the development of the heart, which is NOT correct:
option_a: The heart primordium is initially located in mesenchyme in front of the prochordal plate
option_b: Common cardinal veins empty into the sinus venosus
option_c: The interatrial septum is formed from endocardial cushions, septum primum and septum secundum
option_d: Only cardiac muscle contributes to the interventricular septum
explanation:
Heart development initially occurs in front of the prochordal plate. The common cardinal, vitelline and umbilical veins enter the sinus venosus. The interatrial septum is formed by endocardial cushions, septum primum & septum secundum. The interventricular septum has muscular and membranous parts.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Concerning the truncus ridges, which statement is NOT correct:
option_a: They may grow abnormally and contribute to formation of transposition of the great vessels
option_b: They normally spiral around each other as they grow
option_d: They contribute to the interatrial septum
explanation:
The truncal ridges or swellings are the progenitors of the aorticopulmonary septum within the truncus arteriosus. During development, they spiral, properly orienting the aorta and pulmonary trunks. If they fail to spiral, transposition of the great vessels can occur. They do not involve the interatrial septum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Ostium secundum defect:
option_a: Is characterized by a large opening between left and right atria
option_b: May be caused by excessive resorption of septum primum
option_c: May be caused by inadequate development of septum secundum
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
An ostium secundum defect is a large opening between the atria that can be caused either by excessive resorption of the septum primum or inadequate development of the septum secundum. Depending on the size of the defect, there can be shunting of the blood between the atria.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 164

question_text: Transposition of the great vessels is most directly related to abnormal development of which of the following?
explanation:
The spiral aorticopulmonary septum forms within the truncus arteriosus as the result of the growth of the truncal swellings or ridges.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Which of the following structure is derived from left sixth arterial arch?
explanation:
Explanation:

The left sixth aortic arch gives rise to the ductus arteriosus, which connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta during fetal life, allowing blood to bypass the non-functional fetal lungs. It also contributes to the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery. After birth, the ductus arteriosus closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

Derivatives of arterial arches:

Source of development of main arteries

Key Takeaway:

The left sixth arterial arch gives rise to the ductus arteriosus, facilitating fetal circulation by allowing blood to bypass the lungs, alongside the left pulmonary artery.

question_text: During fetal life and sometimes persisting into the adult there is an opening between the right and left atria; this opening is called the:
explanation:
The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum which exists in the fetus. This opening and the ductus arteriosus serve as two shunts which divert blood away from the developing lungs. Both should close soon after birth. 

The coronary sinus is the large vein on the posterior surface of the heart which drains into the right atrium. It receives blood from the great, middle, and small cardiac veins, the oblique vein of the left atrium, and the left posterior ventricular vein. The sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus are structures in the developing heart that will be covered in embryology.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 217

question_text: The false statement about fetal circulation is:
option_a: Anatomical closure of foramen ovale is by 3 to 5 days
option_b: Anatomical closure of ductus venosus is by 3 to 7 days
option_d: Anatomical closure of ductus arteriosus is by 2 to 3 weeks
explanation:
The anatomical closure of the foramen ovale takes 1 month to a year.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer due to persistence of which arch artery?
explanation:
• The recurrent laryngeal nerves (nerve of 6th pharyngeal arch) initially hook around the sixth arch artery on the respective side.
  • On right side: Because of the distal part of the sixth arch artery disappears, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve moves superiorly and hook around the proximal part of right subclavian artery (the derivatives of 4th arch artery
  • On left side: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the distal part of sixth arch artery, which persists as Ductus arteriosus. When DA obliterates after birth to form ligamentum arteriosus, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the ligamentum arteriosus (left sixth arch artery derivative).

question_text: Which aortic arch forms ligamentum arteriosum?
explanation:
Sixth aortic arch - The right and left arches separate into ventral and dorsal segments. The ventral segments are responsible for the formation of the pulmonary arteries bilaterally. The left ventral arch also contributes to the formation of the pulmonary trunk. The right dorsal arch regresses. The left dorsal arch forms the ductus arteriosus, which later closes and is termed the ligamentum arteriosum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 195

question_text: The most superior part of the inferior vena cava is derived from:
explanation:
The vitelline veins, as they pass through the developing liver, break up into hepatic sinusoids. When the left sinus horn regresses, blood is shunted from the left vitelline vein to the right, which enlarges and ultimately forms the posthepatic portion of the inferior vena cava.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 162

question_text: At birth, the following changes in circulation take place EXCEPT:
option_a: Decrease in pressure in the pleural cavities
explanation:
At birth, the lungs fill with air, and the pressure in the pressure in the pleural cavities begins to decline. Ductus venosus becomes ligamentum venosum. The ductus arteriosus closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Also, the foramen ovale closes and becomes the fossa ovalis.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Which of the following forms the trabeculated part of the right ventricle?
explanation:
The trabeculated part of the right ventricle is formed from the proximal 1/3rd of the bulbus cordis.

The heart tube begins to bend by day 23. This bending creates the cardiac loop.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: At birth, increased pressure in the left atrium is directly caused by:
explanation:
The increased left atrial pressure is directly caused by the closure of the ductus arteriosus, forcing the blood to pass into the lungs and then return in pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The cessation of placental blood flow causes a decrease in systemic pressure and pressure in right atrium, closing foramen ovale.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Which of the following associations are correct?
option_a: Patent ductus arteriosus - left 6th aortic arch
option_b: Double aortic arch - right dorsal aorta
option_c: Double superior vena cava - left anterior cardinal vein
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
A patent ductus involves the left 6th arch. A double aortic arch is caused by persistence of the right dorsal aorta. The common carotid artery is a derivative of the 3rd arch. A double superior vena cava is caused by persistence of part of the left anterior cardinal vein.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Partitioning of the atrium is accomplished by growth of:
explanation:
The growth of both the septum primum and septum secundum contribute to the partitioning of the atrium. Septum primum grows down to meet the endocardial heart cushions, closing foramen primum. Foramen secundum forms within septum primum, and it will be overlapped by the downgrowth of septum secundum, leaving open foramen ovale.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Closure of the foramen primum results from fusion of the:
option_a: Septum secundum and the fused endocardial cushions
option_b: Septum secundum and the septum primum
option_c: Septum primum and the fused endocardial cushions
option_d: Septum primum and the septum spurium
explanation:
The septum primum and the endocardial cushions fuse to close the foramen primum. Subsequently, perforations in the upper part of the septum primum coalesce to form the foramen secundum. It is this foramen that closes postnatally when left atrial pressure equals right atrial pressure.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: Which structure is most important in the formation of the valve of the foramen ovale?
explanation:
The ostium secundum is nearly closed by the growth of the septum secundum, which forms the valve of the foramen ovale. This remains patent until birth, allowing blood to be shunted from right to left atrium. After birth, the closing of ductus arteriosus forces blood into the pulmonary circuit, and the returning blood fills left atrium, balancing the pressure in the right atrium and closing the valve of the foramen ovale.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: If the ductus arteriosus does not spontaneously close off soon after birth (to become the ligamentum arteriosum), it may have to be surgically ligated. When clamping or ligating it, what important structure immediately behind it must be identified and saved?
explanation:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus nerve and loops under the arch of the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum/ductus arteriosis. When performing surgery in this area, like the repair of a patent ductus arteriosis, a surgeon must be very careful to identify and preserve the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. If this nerve is damaged, it may lead to paralysis of the left vocal fold and cause hoarseness in the patient. 

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 217

question_text: What is the location of the foramen secundum?
explanation:
The foramen secundum (ostium secundum) is present at the upper part of the septum primum.

During fetal life, oxygenated blood reaches the right atrium from the placenta. This blood then reaches the left atrium through the gap between the atria. The initial gap is the foramen primum formed at the lower end of the septum primum.

Before the foramen primum is closed, another path has to be created for the flow of blood. This gap is the foramen secundum at the upper part of the septum primum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The most common congenital malformation of the great vessels is:
explanation:
Patent ductus arteriosus is the most common congenital malformation of the great vessels. The ductus arteriosus is the distal portion of the left sixth aortic arch that connects the left pulmonary artery to the aorta.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170
