question_text: Arrange the following structures of the primitive heart tube in cranial to caudal order.
explanation:
The correct order of heart tube structures from cranial to caudal is bulbus cordis, primitive ventricle, primitive atrium, and the sinus venosus.

The 2 heart tubes formed in the cardiogenic area fuse, except in their caudal most end, to become an inverted Y-shaped structure. During this fusion, the central part of the heart tube expands to form the future outflow tract and ventricular regions. The caudal pole of the tube receives the venous drainage, while the cranial end pumps out blood into the arterial system.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The ductus arteriosus sometimes remains open after birth requiring surgical closure. When placing a clamp on the ductus, care must be taken to avoid injury to what important structure immediately dorsal to it?
explanation:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus that wraps around the aorta, posterior to the ductus arteriosus or ligamentum arteriosum. It then travels superiorly to innervate muscles of the larynx. It's important to protect this nerve during surgery! If the left recurrent laryngeal nerve becomes paralyzed, a patient might experience a hoarse voice or even have difficulty breathing due to a laryngeal spasm. You should make sure that you understand what this nerve does, what types of procedures might injure this nerve, and the effects of a damaged left recurrent laryngeal!

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: Which of the embryonic vein does not take part in the formation of the inferior vena cava?
explanation:
Explanation:

The right common cardinal vein does not contribute to the formation of the inferior vena cava (IVC). It forms part of the superior vena cava (SVC) along with the right anterior cardinal vein. Since it is associated with venous return from the upper body, it has no developmental role in any segment of the IVC.

Development of the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC):

  • The IVC is the largest vein in the body, developing from six embryonic components.
  • From caudal to cranial, these components include:
    • Right posterior cardinal vein (Option B):Forms part of the Sacro cardinal segment of the IVC.
    • Right supracardinal vein (Option C):Contributes to the caudal part of the IVC.
    • Right subcardinal vein (Option D):Involved in forming the renal segment of the IVC.
  • Anastomoses: These include connections between the right supracardinal and subcardinal veins, and a channel connecting the right subcardinal vein with the right hepatocardiac channel.
  • Inferior vena cava develops from:
    • Anastomoses of right and left posterior cardinal veins
    • Right supracardinal vein
    • Right suprasubcardinal anastomosis
    • Right subcardinal vein
    • New channel between right subcardinal and cranial part of right vitelline vein
    • Right hepatocardiac channel

Key Takeaway:

The right common cardinal vein does not participate in forming the inferior vena cava, while the right posterior cardinal, right supracardinal, and right subcardinal veins are essential components in its development.

question_text: Sinus venous does not receive blood from which of the following veins?
explanation:
The sinus venosus does not receive blood from the subcardinal veins. They are found in relation to the urogenital ridges and mainly drain the developing kidney.

Sinus venous is the caudal-most part of the tubular heart and has right and left horns. Each horn of sinus venosus has 3 branches:

  • Vitelline vein receives blood from the yolk sac
  • Umbilical vein receives blood from the placenta
  • Common cardinal vein receives blood from the hody wall

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The most common type of cardiac septal defect is:
option_a: Muscular type ventricular septal defect, or VSD
option_b: Secundum type atrial septal defect, or ASD
explanation:
Although the most common ATRIAL septal defect is the secundum type ASD, the overall most common cardiac septal defect is the membranous type VSD.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 171

question_text: The Tetralogy of Fallot includes all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation:
The defects in the Tetralogy of Fallot are pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. The abnormalities result from abnormal conotruncal septation.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 164

question_text: With aortic valvular atresia:
option_a: The left atrium and left ventricle are hyperplastic, or overdeveloped
option_c: Blood passes into the aorta through a patent ductus arteriosus
option_d: Blood fails to reach the descending aorta
explanation:
In order for a patient with an atretic aortic semilunar valve to survive, there must be a patent ductus arteriosus so that blood can reach the systemic circulation. Because the left ventricle is unable to pump, it is HYPOplastic. There is no overriding aorta.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: The crista terminalis is derived from:
option_a: Right horn of the sinus venosus
option_b: Left horn of the sinus venosus
option_d: Right cusp of the valve of the sinus venosus
explanation:
This is pretty picky. Crista terminalis is the ridge on the inner surface of the right atrium that demarcates the smooth walled part derived from sinus venosus and the pectinate muscle-containing part from primitive right atrium. It marks where the right cusp of the sinoatrial valve was before the sinus became part of atrium.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Each horn of sinus venosus receives all the following veins, except;
explanation:
Explanation:

The pulmonary veins do not drain into the sinus venosus at any stage. Instead, the common pulmonary vein forms as an outgrowth from the dorsal wall of the left atrium and becomes incorporated into it, providing the direct venous return from the developing lungs. This separate origin and connection to the left atrium distinguish the pulmonary venous system from the vitelline, umbilical and cardinal systems that empty into the sinus venosus.

Development of the Sinus Venosus:

The sinus venosus is the venous end of the heart tube and is crucial for the development of the heart. It consists of a small transverse body and two horns (right and left).

Vitelline vein (Option A): Drains blood from the yolk sac, supplying nutrients to the embryo. Forms the hepatic portal vein as it persists into postnatal life.

Umbilical vein (Option B): Carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the developing fetus. Plays a vital role in fetal circulation and becomes the round ligament of the liver after birth.

Common cardinal vein (Option D): Drains blood from the body wall into the sinus venosus, integrating systemic venous return into the developing heart. Contributes to the formation of the superior and inferior venacava in postnatal life.

Key Takeaway:

The pulmonary vein is the only vein listed that does not connect to the sinus venosus; it directly enters the left atrium, while the vitelline, umbilical, and common cardinal veins all play integral roles in the early development of the heart and venous system.

question_text: Which of the following adult part of the adult heart is develops from the bulbus cordis?
option_a: Smooth part of the right atrium
option_b: Smooth part of the right ventricle
option_c: Trabeculated part of the right ventricle
option_d: Trabeculated part of the right atrium
explanation:
Explanation:

Bulbus cordis forms the smooth part of the right ventricle (conus arteriosus) and the smooth part of the left ventricle (aortic vestibule).

Other regions:

  • Smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venosus origin)
  • Trabeculated parts of both atria and ventricles come from the primitive atrium and primitive ventricle

Fate of the embryonic dilatations of the primitive heart tube:


Key takeaway: The bulbus cordis contributes to the smooth parts of the ventricles (right - conus arteriosus, left - aortic vestibule).

question_text: The dorsal mesocardium:
option_a: Disappears partially and thereby helps to form the transverse pericardial sinus
option_b: Disappears and helps to form the oblique pericardial sinus
explanation:
Early in heart development, following head folding, the heart tube is suspended within the pericardial cavity by dorsal mesocardium. As the heart folds on itself so that the intake and outflow tracts come together, the dorsal mesocardium ruptures. This forms the transverse pericardial sinus behind the great arteries.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 162

question_text: Each of the following statements are correctly paired EXCEPT:
option_a: Right vitelline vein - inferior vena cava
option_c: Right anterior cardinal vein - part of superior vena cava
option_d: Right umbilical vein - definitive umbilical vein
explanation:
The right umbilical vein totally disappears. The definitive umbilical vein is the left one. After birth, it closes and becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 195

question_text: Which of the following associations are correct?
explanation:
The ligamentum teres hepatis is the remnant of the umbilical vein, and it lies within the falciform ligament, formed from the ventral mesentery. The distal parts of the umbilical arteries close and become medial umbilical ligaments. Ductus venosus becomes ligamentum venosum, and ductus arteriosus becomes ligamentum arteriosum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 169

question_text: Of the following, the one most closely associated with the common carotid artery is:
explanation:
The common carotid artery is from the 3rd aortic arch. The 3rd arch also contributes to the proximal internal carotid artery. The external carotid is a branch of the 3rd arch.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 195

question_text: The remnant of the first aortic arch artery is:
explanation:
First arch becomes maxillary; 2nd arch remnants are stapedial and hyoid arteries; 3rd arch becomes common & proximal internal carotid arteries; 4th arch becomes proximal right subclavian & part of arch of aorta; 6th arch becomes proximal pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 164

question_text: At birth, the distal branches of both internal iliac arteries collapse and persist as the:
explanation:
When the distal parts of the umbilical arteries collapse at birth, they form the medial umbilical ligaments. The urachus persists as the median umbilical ligament. The lateral umbilical folds are peritoneum overlying the inferior epigastric vessels.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: The muscular wall of the esophagus arises from:
explanation:
The muscle of the upper portion of the esophagus is skeletal muscle, derived from branchial arch VI and innervated by recurrent laryngeal branches of vagus nerve, X. The lower part of the esophageal wall is smooth muscle from splanchnic mesoderm, like the rest of the gut wall. It is innervated by parasympathetics from vagus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: In the formation of the pancreas:
option_a: A dorsal and ventral bud from the endoderm of the duodenum are the first indications of a pancreas
option_c: An annular pancreas forms if a portion of the dorsal bud rotates abnormally
option_d: Insulin is not secreted during fetal life
explanation:
Pancreas forms from endodermal diverticula from the hepatic bud and the duodenum. The ventral bud develops into the uncinate process, but if it rotates abnormally it can cause an annular pancreas. Insulin secretion begins around the 5th month of development.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Mesoderm of which of the following structures give rise to the spleen?
explanation:
The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium.

The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi. Later, these lobules fuse to form a single mass of the spleen. The capsule, septa, and connective tissue framework, including reticular fibers, develop from mesoderm. The mesenchymal cells also differentiate into lymphoblasts and other blood-forming cells.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 219

question_text: The liver:
option_a: Receives blood from the placenta via the umbilical vein which runs in the falciform ligament
option_b: Forms as a diverticulum from the foregut endoderm
option_c: Contains hemopoietic and connective tissue cells derived from mesoderm of the septum transversum
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
Liver develops from an endodermal hepatic diverticulum, but also contains mesodermal hemopoietic & connective tissue. Blood from the placenta reaches liver via the left umbilical vein but by-passes the sinusoids through the ductus venosus. The sinusoids are derived from the vitelline veins.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 219

question_text: Identify the shown congenital anomaly in which intestinal loops are present outside the abdominal cavity covered by amniotic membrane?
explanation:
Exomphalos or omphalocele:

  • This anomaly results from failure of coils of the small intestine to return into abdominal cavity from their physiological herniation into extraembryonic coelom during 6th to 10th week of IUL.
  • It occurs in 2.5/10,000 births and could be associated with cardiac and neural tube defects.
  • Clinically, it presents as a rounded mass protruding from the umbilicus. This mass contains coils of the small intestine and is covered by a transparent amniotic membrane.

Reference: Textbook Clinical Embryology by Vishram Singh, 3rd Edition, Page No - 198

question_text: A newborn presented to the NICU with respiratory distress and meconium discharge from the umbilicus. The condition occurs due to the patency of which structure?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A vitelline fistula occurs due to the failure of the vitelline duct (omphalomesenteric duct) to obliterate, leading to meconium discharge from the umbilicus.
  • It connects the midgut to the yolk sac during fetal development, and its persistence results in fecal or intestinal content drainage from the umbilicus.

question_text: A baby after delivery was found to have the following finding shown in image. Which of the following defects in the intrauterine life is the cause of this condition?
option_a: Failure of the intestinal loops to return from umbilicus
option_b: Defective closure of body wall in abdominal region
option_c: Defective closure of body wall in pelvic region
option_d: Defective closure of the vitellointestinal duct
explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of gastroschisis. It is caused due to the failure of the body wall to close in the abdominal region during development.

Ventral wall defects include:

  • Gastroschisis: The intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies to one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Which of the following is NOT associated with esophageal atresia:
option_d: Reflux of milk through nose and mouth, which appears toward the end of the first week after birth
explanation:
Esophageal atresia is thought to result in some cases by abnormal formation of the tracheoesophageal septum. This also explains why esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula are often seen together. Polyhydramnios results from lack of fetal swallowing. Reflux of milk occurs immediately upon first ingestion.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: A newborn boy had no passage of meconium for two days after birth. Examination revealed anal agenesis with perineal fistula. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
option_b: Failure of perforation of anal membrane
option_c: Incomplete separation of cloaca by urorectal septum
option_d: Failure of recanalization of the colon
explanation:
Incomplete separation of cloaca by the urorectal septum causes anal agenesis.

When the urorectal septum is formed, the cloacal membrane gets divided into urogenital membrane anteriorly and anal membrane posteriorly. The ectoderm in the region of the future anal opening is called proctodeum. The proctodeum invaginates and creates the anal pit. The anal membrane now separates the hindgut from the anal pit.

Formation of the anal canal takes place as follows:

  • The upper part of the anal canal is formed by the endodermal hindgut and the lower part by the ectodermal anal pit.
  • The anal membrane in between breaks around the 9th week and the anal canal becomes continuous.
  • The junction between the endodermal and the ectodermal region of the anal canal is marked by the pectinate line.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning the development of the duodenum is FALSE?
option_a: The duodenum rotates to the right side of the embryo during development
option_b: Most of the duodenum becomes retroperitoneal during development
option_c: The duodenum develops only from the caudal foregut
option_d: There is no lumen within the duodenum at some point in development
explanation:
Duodenum develops from caudal foregut and cranial midgut. Except for the short first part and end of the fourth part, the duodenum becomes retroperitoneal after rotating to the right. Epithelial overgrowth temporarily obliterates the duodenal lumen, and duodenal stenosis or atresia may result from failed recanalization.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: In the development of the midgut:
option_a: The superior mesenteric artery is the axis for clockwise rotation of the midgut loop
option_b: The persistence of part of the vitelline duct leads to urachal fistula
option_c: A vitelline cyst may result from abnormal remodelling of the vitelline veins
option_d: An omphalocele is not synonymous with congenital umbilical hernia
explanation:
The midgut rotates in a counterclockwise direction around superior mesenteric artery. Persistence of the vitelline duct may cause a vitelline fistula or cyst. Omphalocele results from a failure of midgut to return to the abdominal cavity, while congenital umbilical hernia is a later herniation of gut through abdominal wall.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 222

question_text: The midgut loop normally herniates through the primitive umbilical ring into the extra-embryonic celom during the 6th-week of development. Failure of the intestinal loops to return to the abdominal cavity by 11th-week results in the formation of which of the following conditions in a baby?
explanation:
Failure of the intestinal loops to return to the abdominal cavity during the 6th to 10th weeks results in omphalocele or exomphalos.

Omphalocele is a congenital malformation in which the abdominal viscera protrudes through a wide umbilical defect. The bowel loops are covered by amnion.

A small omphalocele contains only the intestines. A large omphalocele may contain other viscera such as the stomach, liver, spleen, and large intestine, along with the small intestine. Omphalocele is commonly associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., trisomy 13, trisomy 18, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome) and causes increased levels of a-fetoprotein.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 219

question_text: A persistence of the vitelline duct may result in:
explanation:
If the vitelline duct remains patent, there will be an umbilical or vitelline fistula, leaking meconium or fetal feces at the umbilicus. Partial closure of vitelline duct may result in a vitelline cyst or a Meckel's/ileal diverticulum. The latter are found on the anti-mesenteric side of ileum within 2 feet of cecum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 209

question_text: The fibrous stroma of the liver is derived from which of the following structures?
explanation:
The fibrous stroma of the liver is derived from the septum transversum.

The liver develops as an outgrowth of the endodermal epithelium at the distal end of the foregut. This liver bud or hepatic diverticulum proliferates rapidly and penetrates the septum transversum.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 210

question_text: Which of the following adult structures arises from the embryonic structure indicated in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The marked structure is the allantois, a hindgut diverticulum. It forms the urachus during fetal development, connecting the bladder apex to the umbilicus, which later degenerates into the median umbilical ligament. This ligament runs along the midline of the abdominal wall.


Meckel's diverticulum (Option C): This arises from the vitelline duct, not the urachus.

question_text: Normal gut rotation brings which structure to lie at McBurney's point?
explanation:
McBurney's point, 1/3rd up along a line drawn between anterior superior iliac spine and umbilicus, is a fairly reliable landmark for the appendix. Variations is gut rotation, however, can cause the appendix to be located in other regions.

question_text: In its development, the stomach does NOT:
option_a: Rotate 90 degrees clockwise when viewed from above
explanation:
During its development, the stomach makes a 90 degree rotation clockwise. Different areas of the stomach also grow at different rates, giving it its characteristic shape. Stomach descends as the esophagus grows in length, explaining why thoracic splanchnic nerves to the gut arise from sympathetic ganglia T5-12.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Which of the following develops from the dorsal mesogastrium?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • During embryonic development, the spleen forms from mesenchymal cells within the mesoderm, specifically in the dorsal mesogastrium.

Derivatives of dorsal and ventral mesogastrium

  • During the development of the gut, the stomach is first seen as a fusiform dilatation of the foregut just distal to the oesophagus.
  • Its distal border is attached to the posterior abdominal wall by a fold of peritoneum called the dorsal mesogastrium.The ventral border is attached to the septum transversum by another fold of peritoneum called the ventral mesogastrium.
  • The organsspleen and pancreas develop in the dorsal mesogastrium, and the liver develops in the ventral mesogastrium.

question_text: Of the following, the one most closely associated with the ligamentum teres hepatis is:
explanation:
The ligamentum teres hepatis is the remnant of the umbilical vein after the umbilical vein closes at birth. It can be found in the falciform ligament, a ventral mesentery derivative.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: Which of the following structures is most closely related to the development of both ventral and dorsal mesentery?
explanation:
Ventral mesentery attaches dorsally to the stomach, and is also called ventral mesogastrium. The cranial part of the dorsal mesentery attaches to stomach and is called dorsal mesogastrium.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Digestive System Embryology Page number - 208

question_text: Which portion of the ear is derived from endoderm?
explanation:
The tympanic cavity is endodermal in origin, derived from the 1st pharyngeal pouch. The internal ear, including the cochlea, bony labyrinth and semicircular canals, are derived from the ectodermal otic placode. External auditory meatus, from 1st pharyngeal cleft, is also ectodermal.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Ear Embryology Page number - 321

question_text: Many facial malformations are believed to be due to:
option_a: A failure of the oral membrane to rupture
option_b: A failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the facial processes
option_c: A failure in growth of the head fold
option_d: An abnormal persistence of the pharyngeal clefts
explanation:
Proper migration of neural crest cells into the face area is vitally important to facial development. Neural crest tissue will form much of the facial skeleton.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 275

question_text: Identify the correct associations:
option_a: Primary palate - palatine shelves of maxillary processes
option_c: Nasolacrimal groove - lateral nasal process and mandibular process
option_d: Cleft lip - medial & lateral nasal processes
explanation:
The primary palate arises from the intermaxillary segment. Neural crest cells are vital to the development of the facial swellings. The nasolacrimal groove separates maxillary and lateral nasal swellings. Cleft lip can result from failure of fusion between the maxillary and medial nasal prominences.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 273

question_text: The membranous labyrinth develops from which structure?
explanation:
The membranous labyrinth of the internal ear is derived from the otic vesicle.

The surface ectoderm on either side of the hindbrain thickens to form otic placodes. The otic placodes invaginate to form otic vesicles (auditory vesicles).

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: A newborn presented with the congenital anomaly cleft lip. What is its embryological basis?
option_a: Non fusion of lateral nasal process & maxillary process
option_b: Non fusion of medial nasal process & maxillary process
option_c: Non fusion of palatine shelves cleft palate
option_d: Separation of nasal septum & vomer from palatine process
explanation:
Explanation:

Failure of fusion of the maxillary processes with the medial nasal processes results in cleft lip.

  • By stage 12, migration of the most rostral neural crest cells is complete, initiating the morphogenetic changes that form the face.
  • Localized mesenchymal proliferation produces four paired facial processes: medial nasal, lateral nasal, maxillary, and mandibular.
  • The lateral and medial nasal processes surround the nasal placodes, which sink to form the nasal pits.
  • The medial nasal processes fuse to form the nasal septum, the premaxillary part of the upper lip and jaw, and the primary palate.
  • Maxillary processesgrow toward the medial nasal processes and fuse to complete the upper lip and jaw; failure of this fusion causes unilateral or bilateral cleft lip.
  • The palatine shelvesfrom maxillary processes grow medially and fuse to form the secondary palate; failure of this fusion leads to cleft palate.
  • The lower lip and lower jaw are formed as a result of midline fusion of the mandibular processes, while lateral fusion of the mandibular and maxillary processes forms the commissures of the mouth.

question_text: As a resident in pediatrics, you are called to see a newborn who has a unilateral cleft lip and a unilateral cleft of the primary palate. This condition is most likely the result of:
option_a: Failure of fusion of the mandibular prominences
option_b: Failure of fusion of the medial nasal processes
option_c: Failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence
option_d: Failure of fusion of the lateral palatine processes with the nasal septum
explanation:
This type of cleft is a failure of fusion, or secondary rupture of the union, of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. If the palatine shelves or processes of maxillary prominences rupture or fail to fuse, a midline defect of the secondary palate will result.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 278

question_text: Oblique facial cleft results from failure of fusion between which of the following embryonic processes?
option_c: Medial nasal and lateral nasal processes
explanation:
Explanation:

The oblique facial cleft extends from the upper lip to the medial angle of the eye, along the nasolacrimal groove. It occurs due to failure of fusion between the maxillary process and the lateral nasal process. This defect leaves the nasolacrimal duct exposed.

Cleft lip:

  • Varieties of Cleft Upper Lip:
    • Unilateral Cleft Lip: Caused by failure of fusion between the maxillary process and the medial nasal process on the same side.
    • Bilateral Cleft Lip: Caused by failure of fusion between the maxillary processes and the frontonasal process.
    • Central Cleft Lip (Hair Lip): Results from failure in the development of the philtrum of the upper lip from the frontonasal process.
    • Cleft Lower Lip: Rare occurrence due to failure of fusion of the two mandibular processes in the midline.
  • Medial nasal and maxillary processes fusion (Option A):
    • These processes normally fuse to form the upper lip (particularly the philtrum region).
    • Failure of fusion here causes a cleft lip:
      • If one side fails → Unilateral cleft lip
      • If both sides fail → Bilateral cleft lip
    • It does not produce an oblique cleft extending toward the eye.
  • Medial nasal and lateral nasal processes fusion (Option C):
    • Fusion between these forms the bridge and dorsum of the nose.
    • Failure of fusion here leads to a median nasal cleft (or median cleft lip if involving lower portions).
    • It affects the midline, not the oblique facial region.
  • Right and left maxillary processes fusion (Option D):
    • The maxillary processes form the upper cheeks and lateral parts of the upper jaw.
    • They do not normally fuse with each other in the midline instead, each fuse with the medial nasal process.
    • Therefore, their non-fusion does not produce a typical facial cleft.

Oblique Facial Cleft (Orbitofacial Fissure):

  • A rare congenital anomaly where the maxillary process fails to fuse with the lateral nasal process.
  • The fissure extends from the medial angle of the eye to the upper lip.
  • This condition exposes the nasolacrimal duct to the exterior and is usually bilateral.

Key takeaways:

Cleft upper lip can be unilateral, bilateral, or central, while oblique facial cleft, a rare anomaly, occurs due to the failure of fusion between the maxillary and lateral nasal processes, exposing the nasolacrimal duct.

question_text: The otic vesicle does NOT develop into the:
explanation:
Otic vesicle develops into the saccule, cochlear duct or membranous cochlea, utricle, semicircular canals and endolymphatic duct & sac. It develops FROM the ectodermal otic placode.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Ear Embryology Page number - 321

question_text: From which structures do the alae of the nose develop?
explanation:
The alae of the nose develop from the lateral nasal processes.

The development of various components of the nose can be summarized as follows:

  • Bridge - The frontonasal process
  • Dorsum and tip - Fused medial nasal processes
  • Alae - The lateral nasal processes
  • Anterior nares (nostrils) - The original site of the nasal pit

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: The condition shown in the image arises due to the failure of fusion between which embryological prominences?
option_a: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
option_b: Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
option_c: Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
option_d: Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
explanation:
Explanation:

  • During embryological development of the face, the medial nasal prominence must fuse with the maxillary prominence to form the upper lip and part of the palate.
  • Failure of this fusion leads to a cleft lip (split in the upper lip) and possibly a cleft palate (split in the roof of the mouth).
  • These anomalies can be unilateral or bilateral and vary in severity.

Explanation of other options:

Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence (Option A): Failure leads to an oblique facial cleft, not a cleft lip/palate.

Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence (Option B): These prominences normally do not fuse; hence, failure is not related to cleft lip/palate.

Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence (Option D): Non-fusion can cause other facial malformations, but not cleft lip/palate.

question_text: Which structures are derived from the optic cup?
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
The optic cup ultimately develops into the pigment layer of the retina, the neural retina, the epithelium of the iris and the epithelium of the ciliary body.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 268

question_text: Which structures are derived from the intermaxillary segment of the embryonic face?
option_b: Anterior portion of the upper jaws
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
The intermaxillary segment gives rise to the philtrum, the upper incisors, the anterior portion of the upper jaws, and the primary palate, which lies anteriorly.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 275

question_text: The defect shown in image below is due to the failure of fusion between which structures?
option_a: Non-fusion of palatine processes with premaxilla only
option_b: Non-fusion of palatine processes in midline only
option_c: Non-fusion of palatine process with premaxilla and with each other
option_d: Non-fusion of median nasal process with maxillary process
explanation:
Bilateral complete cleft palate is due to the non-fusion of palatine processes with the premaxilla and with each other.

The palate is formed from two main structures:

  • Primary palate: The small triangular anterior part of the palate is formed by the fused medial nasal processes (intermaxillary segment or premaxilla).
  • Secondary palate: The main part of the palate is formed by the 2 palatine processes that converge from the maxillary processes

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Head and Neck Embryology Page number - 278

question_text: True about defect shown below is
option_a: Is the result of failure of the cephalic part of the neural tube to form
option_b: Has its inception during the 5th week of development
option_c: Is seen more frequently in females than in males
option_d: Is accompanied by a deficiency in amniotic fluid
explanation:
Anencephaly occurs when the cephalic part of the neural tube fails to close. The reflex to swallow amniotic fluid does not develop and excess amniotic fluid, or polyhydramnios, results. It is 4 times more common in females than in males. Neural tube forms from the fusion of neural folds during the 4th week.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Central Nervous System Embryology Page number - 288

question_text: In the development of the nervous system:
option_a: The neural groove forms from the neural plate
option_b: The neural folds are composed of neuroepithelial cells
option_c: The neural tube maintains temporary contact with the amniotic cavity via neuropores
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
The neural groove forms from the neural plate when lateral parts of the plate elevate to form neural folds. Neural folds are composed of neuroepithelium which gives rise to neuroblasts, gliablasts & ependymal cells. After the neural tube forms, it maintains contact with the amniotic cavity via cranial & caudal neuropores.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Central Nervous System Embryology Page number - 287

question_text: With respect to the nervous system, which of the following is NOT correct:
option_a: A muscle's nerve supply can be used as an indicator of its level of origin and path of migration

question_text: At the third week of intrauterine life the Rathke's pouch gives rise to development of which of the following structure?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The pituitary gland develops from two distinct parts:
  • Adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) develops from Rathke's pouch, which is an ectodermal evagination from the roof of the primitive oral cavity (stomodeum). Rathke's pouch forms around the third week of intrauterine life.
  • Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) arises from the neuroectoderm of the hypothalamus (floor of the third ventricle).
  • Adenohypophysis gives rise to:
  • Pars anterior (anterior lobe), which forms a major part of the anterior pituitary.
  • Pars intermedia, which is formed from the posterior wall of Rathke's pouch.
  • Pars tuberalis, an upward extension along the infundibular stalk.
  • Neurohypophysis forms the pars posterior (posterior lobe/pars nervosa) and infundibulum.

Thyroid gland develops from the thyroglossal duct, an endodermal structure (Option A).

Parathyroid gland arises from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches (option B).

Pineal gland (develops from a diverticulum in the roof of the third ventricle (Option C).

Key takeaway:

Rathke's pouch forms the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary), while the other structures develop from different embryological origins.

question_text: In the development of the nervous system:
